response: {"text":"A fundamental idea in the theory of gravitation claims that the force of gravity and the resistance to acceleration are the same thing, so they should behave identically. To check this, researchers used solid pieces whose physical properties change with direction—anisotropic crystals. If gravity behaved like other directional properties, its pull would vary when the crystal was turned; if it follows the theory, the weight should stay the same regardless of orientation. Large samples representing five distinct crystal structures were weighed with the Earth in several axial positions, using a balance capable of detecting changes as small as one part in a billion. All measurements showed no directional dependence, supporting the equivalence principle to the stated precision. The experiment also demonstrated that such extreme accuracy is achievable with a gravity balance even when the test mass must be rotated."}
